title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.2

hero.subtitle: The cryptographic protocol that secured the internet for a decade, providing privacy and data integrity between applications.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
TLS 1.2 provides communication security over the Internet. The protocol allows client/server applications to communicate in a way that is designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, or message forgery.

TLS 1.2 was the dominant secure transport protocol from 2008 until TLS 1.3 was standardized in 2018. It remains widely deployed and supported.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS 1.2 secures communication between a client and a server over the Internet. It is designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery. It was the dominant secure transport protocol from 2008 until TLS 1.3 was standardized in 2018.

sections.title: Handshake Protocol
sections.content:
The TLS handshake negotiates security parameters, authenticates the server (and optionally the client), and establishes shared keys for encryption.

ClientHelloClient sends its highest supported protocol version, cipher suites, and a random value
ServerHelloServer selects the cipher suite and sends its own random value (the certificate follows in a separate Certificate message)
ServerKeyExchangeAdditional key material for DHE/ECDHE cipher suites
ClientKeyExchangeClient sends pre-master secret (encrypted with server's public key)
ChangeCipherSpecBoth sides switch to the negotiated encryption
FinishedVerification that the handshake was not tampered with
sections.plainLanguage: The handshake comes first. The client and server agree on security settings, the server proves its identity (and optionally the client does too), and both derive shared encryption keys. Each side then switches to encryption, and a Finished message verifies that nobody tampered with the handshake.

sections.title: Record Protocol
sections.content:
The TLS Record Protocol takes messages to be transmitted, fragments the data into manageable blocks, optionally compresses, applies a MAC, encrypts, and transmits the result.

TLS Record Format
+------+------+------+----------+
| Type | Ver  | Len  | Fragment |
| (1)  | (2)  | (2)  | (varies) |
+------+------+------+----------+
Content Typehandshake(22), application_data(23), alert(21), change_cipher_spec(20)
VersionTLS 1.2 = {3, 3}
LengthMax 2^14 bytes per record
sections.plainLanguage: After the handshake, the Record Protocol carries the data. It splits data into blocks of at most 2^14 bytes, optionally compresses them, adds a message authentication code (MAC, a check value that detects changes), and encrypts. Each record has a header giving its type, version and length.

sections.title: Cipher Suites
sections.content:
TLS 1.2 introduced support for SHA-256 as the default hash, authenticated encryption with AEAD cipher modes, and more flexible cipher suite negotiation.

Common TLS 1.2 Cipher Suites
TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA256
TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256
TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256

ECDHE cipher suites provide forward secrecy: compromising the server's long-term key does not compromise past session keys.
sections.plainLanguage: A cipher suite is a named set of algorithms for key exchange, encryption and integrity checking, such as TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384. TLS 1.2 added SHA-256 as the default hash and authenticated encryption modes. ECDHE suites give forward secrecy, so a stolen server key does not expose past sessions.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
BEAST Attack
CBC cipher vulnerability mitigated by 1/n-1 record splitting
POODLE
Padding oracle attack on SSL 3.0 CBC that led to SSL 3.0 being disabled
Lucky 13
Timing attack on CBC mode MACs, mitigated in constant-time implementations
Forward Secrecy
ECDHE key exchange provides forward secrecy, now considered essential
sections.plainLanguage: Researchers have found attacks on older TLS and SSL features: BEAST and Lucky 13 against CBC encryption mode, and POODLE against SSL 3.0, which led to SSL 3.0 being disabled. Mitigations exist, and ECDHE key exchange, which provides forward secrecy, is now considered essential.

references.text: Dierks, T. and E. Rescorla, "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.2", RFC 5246, August 2008.
Dierks, T. and C. Allen, "The TLS Protocol Version 1.0", RFC 2246, January 1999.
Rescorla, E., "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3", RFC 8446, August 2018.

summary: TLS 1.2 lets two programs talk over an untrusted network without being overheard, altered or forged. A handshake agrees on a cipher suite and shared keys and authenticates the server, then a record layer protects the data. It replaced TLS 1.1 and was itself replaced by TLS 1.3, but remains widely deployed.

plainLanguage.summary: TLS 1.2 lets two programs communicate over an untrusted network without being overheard, altered or forged. A handshake agrees on a cipher suite and shared keys and authenticates the server. A record layer then protects the data. It replaced TLS 1.1, was itself replaced by TLS 1.3, and remains widely deployed.

tldr.problem: Applications talking over the Internet can be eavesdropped on, altered or impersonated.
tldr.mechanism: A handshake negotiates a cipher suite, authenticates the server with a certificate and derives shared keys; a record layer then fragments, authenticates and encrypts the data.
tldr.outcome: It secured most web traffic for about a decade, but its legacy options (CBC, RSA key transport) led to attacks and TLS 1.3 replaced it.

what is the tls record protocol
what is forward secrecy in tls
today: TLS 1.2 is still supported by almost every server and client, and many sites accept it alongside TLS 1.3. Modern guidance restricts it to ECDHE key exchange and AEAD cipher suites such as AES-GCM, and avoids the CBC and RSA key-transport suites that earlier attacks targeted. New designs should prefer TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446).
